claim: Homeostatic synaptic plasticity is a non-Hebbian synaptic mechanism that adjusts synaptic strength to maintain network stability while achieving optimal information processing.
source: Homeostatic synaptic plasticity is a non-Hebbian synaptic mechanism that adjusts synaptic strength to maintain network stability while achieving optimal information processing.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about homeostatic synaptic plasticity that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Synaptic signaling through retinoic acid (RA) and its receptor, RARα, has been shown to be critically involved in the homeostatic adjustment of synaptic transmission in both hippocampus and sensory cortices.
source: Among the molecular mediators shown to regulate this form of plasticity, synaptic signaling through retinoic acid (RA) and its receptor, RARα, has been shown to be critically involved in the homeostatic adjustment of synaptic transmission in both hippocampus and sensory cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chen et al., 2014) as indicated in the context.

claim: RARα binds to a subset of dendritically sorted brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) mRNA splice isoforms and represses their translation.
source: We show that RARα binds to a subset of dendritically sorted brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) mRNA splice isoforms and represses their translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-binding assays and synaptoneurosome experiments presented in Figure 2.

claim: RA-mediated translational de-repression of postsynaptic BDNF results in the retrograde activation of presynaptic tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) receptors.
source: The RA-mediated translational de-repression of postsynaptic BDNF results in the retrograde activation of presynaptic tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) receptors, facilitating presynaptic homeostatic compensation through enhanced presynaptic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: RA-mediated translational de-repression of postsynaptic BDNF facilitates presynaptic homeostatic compensation through enhanced presynaptic release.
source: The RA-mediated translational de-repression of postsynaptic BDNF results in the retrograde activation of presynaptic tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) receptors, facilitating presynaptic homeostatic compensation through enhanced presynaptic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSC frequency data and PPR measurements presented in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Chronic synaptic inactivity at glutamatergic synapses triggers RA synthesis in neuronal dendrites.
source: Chronic synaptic inactivity at glutamatergic synapses triggers RA synthesis in neuronal dendrites, which in turn drives local synthesis and synaptic incorporation of GluA1 containing α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) and concomitant removal of γ-aminobutyric acid receptors (GABAARs) from inhibitory synapses, thus restoring synaptic excitatory/inhibitory balance (Aoto et al., 2008; Sarti et al., 2013; Maghsoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Aoto et al., 2008; Sarti et al., 2013; Maghsoodi et al., 2008).

claim: RA synthesis in neuronal dendrites drives local synthesis and synaptic incorporation of GluA1 containing AMPARs.
source: Chronic synaptic inactivity at glutamatergic synapses triggers RA synthesis in neuronal dendrites, which in turn drives local synthesis and synaptic incorporation of GluA1 containing α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) and concomitant removal of γ-aminobutyric acid receptors (GABAARs) from inhibitory synapses, thus restoring synaptic excitatory/inhibitory balance (Aoto et al., 2008; Sarti et al., 2013; Maghsoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Aoto et al., 2008; Sarti et al., 2013; Maghsoodi et al., 2008).

claim: RA synthesis in neuronal dendrites drives concomitant removal of GABAARs from inhibitory synapses.
source: Chronic synaptic inactivity at glutamatergic synapses triggers RA synthesis in neuronal dendrites, which in turn drives local synthesis and synaptic incorporation of GluA1 containing α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) and concomitant removal of γ-aminobutyric acid receptors (GABAARs) from inhibitory synapses, thus restoring synaptic excitatory/inhibitory balance (Aoto et al., 2008; Sarti et al., 2013; Maghsoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Aoto et al., 2008; Sarti et al., 2013; Maghsoodi et al., 2008).

claim: RARα is a nuclear receptor that mediates RA-dependent transcriptional activation during development.
source: The RA receptor RARα is a nuclear receptor that mediates RA-dependent transcriptional activation during development (Chambon, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chambon, 1996.

claim: In mature neurons, RARα translocates out of the nucleus and acts as a molecular mediator for RA-dependent de novo protein synthesis.
source: In mature neurons, however, RARα translocates out of the nucleus and acts as a molecular mediator for RA-dependent de novo protein synthesis (Poon and Chen, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poon and Chen, 2008.

claim: RARα binds to mRNAs via specific sequence motifs and mediates the translation of these mRNAs in an RA-dependent manner in the context of homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
source: In the context of homeostatic synaptic plasticity, RARα has been shown to bind to mRNAs via specific sequence motifs, and mediate the translation of these mRNAs in an RA-dependent manner.
evidence: This statement references established findings from previous work.

claim: Activation of GluA1 synthesis upon chronic synaptic activity blockade requires both RA synthesis and normal RARα expression.
source: For example, activation of GluA1 synthesis upon chronic synaptic activity blockade has been demonstrated to require both RA synthesis and normal RARα expression (Aoto et al., 2008; Maghsoodi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Aoto et al., 2008; Maghsoodi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: Changes in presynaptic functions (i.e. release probability) as part of homeostatic synaptic mechanism have been documented in multiple organisms.
source: Additionally, changes in presynaptic functions (i.e. release probability) as part of homeostatic synaptic mechanism have also been documented in multiple organisms (Wang et al., 2011; Lindskog et al., 2010; Thiagarajan et al., 2005; Davis and Müller, 2015; Murthy et al., 2001; Gong et al., 2007; Jakawich et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: BDNF was found to be involved in the homeostatic regulation of presynaptic release in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: One of the classical synaptic retrograde messengers, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), was found to be involved in the homeostatic regulation of presynaptic release in cultured hippocampal neurons (Jakawich et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jakawich et al., 2010.

claim: Postsynaptic AMPAR blockade-induced activation of RA signaling has been implicated in dendritic protein synthesis in the context of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Moreover, both postsynaptic AMPAR blockade-induced activation of RA signaling and the phospholipase D (PLD)-mTORC1 signaling pathway have been implicated in dendritic protein synthesis in the context of homeostatic plasticity (Henry et al., 2012; Henry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henry et al., 2012 and Henry et al., 2018.

claim: The phospholipase D (PLD)-mTORC1 signaling pathway has been implicated in dendritic protein synthesis in the context of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Moreover, both postsynaptic AMPAR blockade-induced activation of RA signaling and the phospholipase D (PLD)-mTORC1 signaling pathway have been implicated in dendritic protein synthesis in the context of homeostatic plasticity (Henry et al., 2012; Henry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henry et al., 2012 and Henry et al., 2018.

claim: In older (21 days in vitro [DIV]) but not younger (14 DIV) cultured primary hippocampal neurons, chronic treatment with postsynaptic activity blockers results in a significant increase in both mEPSC frequency and mEPSC amplitude.
source: We have previously shown that in older (21 days in vitro [DIV]) but not younger (14 DIV) cultured primary hippocampal neurons, chronic treatment with postsynaptic activity blockers such as the AMPAR antagonist 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) or L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel (VDCC) inhibitor nifedipine results in a significant increase in both mEPSC frequency and mEPSC amplitude (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The increase in mEPSC amplitude is observed in both young and old cultured neurons.
source: Thus, consistent with the literature, while the increase in mEPSC amplitude is observed in both young and old cultured neurons, the enhancement in frequency is only present in the older cultures (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The enhancement in mEPSC frequency is only present in older cultures.
source: Thus, consistent with the literature, while the increase in mEPSC amplitude is observed in both young and old cultured neurons, the enhancement in frequency is only present in the older cultures (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The increase in both mEPSC frequency and amplitude requires RA synthesis as pharmacological inhibition of RA synthesis blocks the increase in both parameters.
source: Importantly, this increase in both mEPSC frequency and amplitude requires RA synthesis as pharmacological inhibition of RA synthesis blocks the increase in both parameters.
evidence: This claim references previous experimental findings.

claim: RA synthesis in postsynaptic neurons triggers presynaptic changes in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Additionally, RA synthesis in postsynaptic neurons triggers presynaptic changes in a cell-autonomous manner as sparse expression of a dihydropyridine-insensitive L-VDCC, which specifically blocks RA synthesis in transfected postsynaptic neurons, prevented the nifedipine-induced homeostatic increase in mEPSC frequency.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental evidence from previous work involving sparse expression of dihydropyridine-insensitive L-VDCC.

claim: Acute RA treatment (10 μM, 4 hr) significantly increases both mEPSC amplitude and frequency in CA1 pyramidal neurons from 21–25 DIV organotypic cultured hippocampal slices.
source: A significant increase in both mEPSC amplitude and frequency in CA1 pyramidal neurons was observed (Figure 1A and B), replicating our previous findings in primary hippocampal neuronal cultures (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: RA treatment significantly reduces paired-pulse ratios (PPRs) of evoked EPSCs, suggesting potential enhancement of presynaptic function by RA.
source: RA treatment significantly reduced the PPRs, suggesting potential enhancement of presynaptic function by RA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The failure rates of eEPSCs were comparable between –60 and +40 mV in both DMSO- and RA-treated slices, indicating little if any presence of postsynaptic silent synapses.
source: The failure rates were comparable between –60 and +40 mV in both DMSO- and RA-treated slices, indicating little if any presence of postsynaptic silent synapses in these slices, and that activation of postsynaptic silent synapses is not a contributing factor to the mEPSC frequency changes observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation of postsynaptic silent synapses is not a contributing factor to the mEPSC frequency changes observed.
source: The failure rates were comparable between –60 and +40 mV in both DMSO- and RA-treated slices, indicating little if any presence of postsynaptic silent synapses in these slices, and that activation of postsynaptic silent synapses is not a contributing factor to the mEPSC frequency changes observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the failure rate data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: New synapse formation is unlikely to underlie the mEPSC frequency increase.
source: Moreover, given that the mEPSC frequency increase only occurs in older slices, but not in younger ones where synaptogenesis is more robust, we think it is unlikely that new synapse formation underlies frequency increase.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that frequency increases occur only in older slices.

claim: Modification of presynaptic release is a conserved homeostatic mechanism operating at glutamatergic synapses across species.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with previous findings from both rodent and Drosophila studies (Davis and Müller, 2015; Jakawich et al., 2010; Subramanian and Dickman, 2015; Bergquist et al., 2010) and demonstrate that modification of presynaptic release is a conserved homeostatic mechanism operating at glutamatergic synapses across species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Davis and Müller, 2015; Jakawich et al., 2010; Subramanian and Dickman, 2015; Bergquist et al., 2010).

claim: Selective deletion of RARα in postsynaptic neurons (Cre expressed in CA1 neurons), but not presynaptic neurons (Cre expressed in CA3 neurons), blocks RA-induced homeostatic increases in both mEPSC amplitude and frequency.
source: Selective deletion of RARα in postsynaptic neurons (Cre expressed in CA1 neurons), but not presynaptic neurons (Cre expressed in CA3 neurons), blocked RA-induced homeostatic increases in both mEPSC amplitude and frequency (Figure 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Selective deletion of RARα in postsynaptic neurons blocks CNQX-induced homeostatic increases in both mEPSC amplitude and frequency.
source: Importantly, these results were also observed when homeostatic plasticity was induced with chronic synaptic activity blocker CNQX (20 µM, 36 hr) (Figure 1C), which has been shown to induce de novo RA synthesis (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: CNQX has been shown to induce de novo RA synthesis.
source: Importantly, these results were also observed when homeostatic plasticity was induced with chronic synaptic activity blocker CNQX (20 µM, 36 hr) (Figure 1C), which has been shown to induce de novo RA synthesis (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Newly synthesized RA acts via postsynaptic RARα to promote homeostatic adjustment of synaptic strength in both pre- and postsynaptic compartments.
source: Thus, newly synthesized RA acts via postsynaptic RARα to promote homeostatic adjustment of synaptic strength in both pre- and postsynaptic compartments.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing postsynaptic RARα deletion blocks both pre- and postsynaptic changes.

claim: RARα signaling mediates homeostatic plasticity at inhibitory synapses.
source: RARα signaling has also been shown to mediate homeostatic plasticity at inhibitory synapses (Sarti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sarti et al., 2013.

claim: Acute RA treatment in 21–25 DIV cultured slices significantly reduces mIPSC amplitudes.
source: Acute RA treatment in 21–25 DIV cultured slices significantly reduced mIPSC amplitudes as has been shown in younger slices (Sarti et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and citation to Sarti et al., 2013.

claim: In older neurons (21-25 DIV), the mIPSC frequency is reduced by RA.
source: Interestingly, unlike those in younger neurons, the mIPSC frequency in these older neurons was also reduced by RA.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation comparing older and younger neurons.

claim: Changes in inhibitory synaptic transmission induced by RA are blocked by postsynaptic RARα deletion.
source: These changes in inhibitory synaptic transmission were blocked by postsynaptic RARα deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Visual deprivation reduces both mIPSC amplitude and frequency in post-critical period layer 2/3 visual cortical neurons.
source: This result is consistent with our previous observations showing that visual deprivation reduces both mIPSC amplitude and frequency in post-critical period layer 2/3 visual cortical neurons (Zhong et al., 2018), indicating that the impact of RA on inhibitory synaptic transmission may be conserved across different brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhong et al., 2018.

claim: The impact of RA on inhibitory synaptic transmission may be conserved across different brain regions.
source: This result is consistent with our previous observations showing that visual deprivation reduces both mIPSC amplitude and frequency in post-critical period layer 2/3 visual cortical neurons (Zhong et al., 2018), indicating that the impact of RA on inhibitory synaptic transmission may be conserved across different brain regions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing results across different brain regions.

claim: BDNF is synthesized as a proneurotrophin known as proBDNF and secreted as a mixture of proBDNF and mature BDNF processed from proBDNF.
source: It is synthesized as a proneurotrophin known as proBDNF and secreted as a mixture of proBDNF and mature BDNF processed from proBDNF (Foltran and Diaz, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Foltran and Diaz, 2016.

claim: Retrograde BDNF-TrkB signaling has been well established in modulating both Hebbian synaptic plasticity and homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
source: The retrograde BDNF-TrkB signaling has been well established in modulating both Hebbian synaptic plasticity (Andero et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2018) and homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Jakawich et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Andero et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2018; Jakawich et al., 2010).

claim: BDNF expression in the brain is developmentally regulated and exhibits a steep increase between postnatal day 15 and 20.
source: BDNF expression in the brain is developmentally regulated and exhibits a steep increase between postnatal day 15 and 20 (Schoups et al., 1995; Dincheva et al., 2016), a time period that coincides with the emergence of RA-dependent presynaptic homeostatic modulation observed in 21 DIV primary cultured hippocampal neurons (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schoups et al., 1995 and Dincheva et al., 2016.

claim: The developmental increase in BDNF expression between postnatal day 15 and 20 coincides with the emergence of RA-dependent presynaptic homeostatic modulation observed in 21 DIV primary cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: BDNF expression in the brain is developmentally regulated and exhibits a steep increase between postnatal day 15 and 20 (Schoups et al., 1995; Dincheva et al., 2016), a time period that coincides with the emergence of RA-dependent presynaptic homeostatic modulation observed in 21 DIV primary cultured hippocampal neurons (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal correlation between BDNF expression and homeostatic modulation.

claim: Immunoblotting of proBDNF in hippocampal tissue collected at different developmental stages shows a gradual increase in BDNF expression during the first 4 postnatal weeks.
source: Immunoblotting of proBDNF in hippocampal tissue collected at different developmental stages showed a gradual increase in BDNF expression during the first 4 postnatal weeks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression of BDNF gradually increases as organotypic hippocampal slice cultures mature from 1 to 21 DIV.
source: Immunoblot analysis from cultured hippocampal slices (prepared from postnatal day 8 mouse pups) showed a similar trend where the expression of BDNF gradually increases as the cultures mature from 1 to 21 DIV (Figure 2A), suggesting that this developmental upregulation of BDNF expression is preserved in our organotypic hippocampal slice culture system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The developmental upregulation of BDNF expression is preserved in organotypic hippocampal slice culture system.
source: Immunoblot analysis from cultured hippocampal slices (prepared from postnatal day 8 mouse pups) showed a similar trend where the expression of BDNF gradually increases as the cultures mature from 1 to 21 DIV (Figure 2A), suggesting that this developmental upregulation of BDNF expression is preserved in our organotypic hippocampal slice culture system.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In rodents, the Bdnf gene consists of nine unique promoters (on nine separate exons) that drive the expression of several distinct Bdnf transcript isoforms.
source: In rodents, the Bdnf gene represents a complex structure that consists of nine unique promoters (on nine separate exons) that drive the expression of several distinct Bdnf transcript isoforms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the Bdnf gene structure, supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All regulatory non-coding exons of the Bdnf gene yield a single identical mature BDNF protein.
source: All regulatory non-coding exons yield a single identical mature BDNF protein (Aid et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aid et al., 2007.

claim: At least two Bdnf exons (exon 2 and exon 6) carry RARα-binding motifs in their sequence.
source: This analysis revealed that at least two Bdnf exons (exon 2 and exon 6) carry RARα-binding motifs in their sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico analysis results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bdnf transcripts containing exon 2 or exon 6 are trafficked to distal dendrites and are subject to synaptic activity-dependent translational regulation.
source: Bdnf transcripts containing exon 2 or exon 6 are trafficked to distal dendrites and are subject to synaptic activity-dependent translational regulation (Song et al., 2017; Baj et al., 2011; Colliva and Tongiorgi, 2021; Vaghi et al., 2014; Baj, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: In cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons, the localization of Bdnf exon 2 and exon 6 in distal dendrites increases dramatically as the culture matures from 7 to 18 DIV.
source: In cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons, the localization of Bdnf exon 2 and exon 6 in distal dendrites increases dramatically as the culture matures from 7 to 18 DIV (Baj et al., 2011), making them potential targets for RA/RARα-mediated translational regulation around the onset time of homeostatic presynaptic changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Baj et al., 2011.

claim: Bdnf exon 2 and exon 6 are potential targets for RA/RARα-mediated translational regulation around the onset time of homeostatic presynaptic changes.
source: In cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons, the localization of Bdnf exon 2 and exon 6 in distal dendrites increases dramatically as the culture matures from 7 to 18 DIV (Baj et al., 2011), making them potential targets for RA/RARα-mediated translational regulation around the onset time of homeostatic presynaptic changes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal correlation between dendritic localization and homeostatic changes.

claim: The carboxyl-terminal F domain of RARα mediates direct binding to substrate mRNAs.
source: Specifically, the carboxyl-terminal F domain of RARα mediates direct binding to substrate mRNAs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim references established findings from previous work, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: RARβ shows only minimal association with dendritic mRNAs.
source: This mRNA-binding ability is specific to RARα as another RA receptor family member RARβ, which has a different amino acid sequence in the F domain, shows only minimal association with dendritic mRNAs (Poon and Chen, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poon and Chen, 2008.

claim: Bdnf transcripts containing exon 2 or exon 6 exhibit selective enrichment through binding to RARα LBD.
source: Bdnf transcripts containing exon 2 or exon 6 exhibited selective enrichment through binding to RARα LBD, along with Gria1 mRNAs, an mRNA substrate of RARα identified in our previous study (Poon and Chen, 2008; Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-binding assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Gria1 mRNAs are an mRNA substrate of RARα.
source: Bdnf transcripts containing exon 2 or exon 6 exhibited selective enrichment through binding to RARα LBD, along with Gria1 mRNAs, an mRNA substrate of RARα identified in our previous study (Poon and Chen, 2008; Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poon and Chen, 2008.

claim: Bdnf transcript containing exon 1 does not bind to RARα LBD.
source: By contrast, Bdnf transcript containing exon 1 that carries only a single RARα recognition motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and is not sorted to dendrites in hippocampal neurons (Baj et al., 2011) failed to bind to RARα LBD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Baj et al., 2011.

claim: Bdnf transcript containing exon 1 is not sorted to dendrites in hippocampal neurons.
source: By contrast, Bdnf transcript containing exon 1 that carries only a single RARα recognition motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and is not sorted to dendrites in hippocampal neurons (Baj et al., 2011) failed to bind to RARα LBD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Baj et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of F domain abolishes the binding activity of all mRNAs to RARα.
source: Additionally, deletion of F domain, the mRNA-binding domain at the C-terminal end of RARα, abolished the binding activity of all mRNAs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The two dendritically localized Bdnf mRNAs (carrying exon 2 and exon 6) exhibit specific binding to RARα F domain.
source: Taken together, this data indicates that the two dendritically localized Bdnf mRNAs (carrying exon 2 and exon 6) exhibit specific binding to RARα F domain.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-binding assay results.

claim: A brief treatment of synaptoneurosomes with 1 μM RA for 30 min at 37°C significantly increases GluA1 protein levels.
source: A brief treatment of synaptoneurosomes with 1 μM RA for 30 min at 37°C significantly increased GluA1 protein levels and demonstrated the translational competency of the synaptoneurosomal preparation (Aoto et al., 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and citation to Aoto et al., 2008.

claim: The expression levels of proBDNF protein increase significantly following 30 min RA treatment of synaptoneurosomes.
source: Importantly, the expression levels of proBDNF protein also increased significantly (Figure 2E) while PSD95, whose mRNAs are also dendritically localized but do not bind to RARα, failed to respond to RA stimulation (Poon and Chen, 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PSD95 mRNAs are dendritically localized but do not bind to RARα.
source: Importantly, the expression levels of proBDNF protein also increased significantly (Figure 2E) while PSD95, whose mRNAs are also dendritically localized but do not bind to RARα, failed to respond to RA stimulation (Poon and Chen, 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poon and Chen, 2008.

claim: PSD95 protein levels fail to respond to RA stimulation in synaptoneurosomes.
source: Importantly, the expression levels of proBDNF protein also increased significantly (Figure 2E) while PSD95, whose mRNAs are also dendritically localized but do not bind to RARα, failed to respond to RA stimulation (Poon and Chen, 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and citation to Poon and Chen, 2008.

claim: RARα binding to Bdnf mRNAs conveys translational regulation of BDNF by RA.
source: Thus, RARα binding to Bdnf mRNAs does convey translational regulation of BDNF by RA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the synaptoneurosome translation experiments.

claim: Acute RA treatment or prolonged CNQX treatment significantly increases both mEPSC amplitudes and frequencies in uninfected control slices.
source: Acute RA treatment or prolonged CNQX treatment significantly increased both mEPSC amplitudes and frequencies in uninfected control slices (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Presynaptic deletion of BDNF does not impair RA-induced or CNQX-induced changes in mEPSCs.
source: While presynaptic deletion of BDNF did not impair either of these changes in mEPSCs, postsynaptic deletion of BDNF prevented the increase in mEPSC frequency (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: Postsynaptic deletion of BDNF prevents the increase in mEPSC frequency induced by RA or CNQX.
source: While presynaptic deletion of BDNF did not impair either of these changes in mEPSCs, postsynaptic deletion of BDNF prevented the increase in mEPSC frequency (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: Presynaptic, but not postsynaptic deletion of TrkB blocks the increase in mEPSC frequency induced by either RA or CNQX.
source: By contrast, presynaptic, but not postsynaptic deletion of TrkB blocked the increase in frequency induced by either RA or CNQX (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Deletion of either BDNF or TrkB pre- or postsynaptically does not affect the homeostatic increase in mEPSC amplitude.
source: Deletion of either BDNF or TrkB pre- or postsynaptically did not affect the homeostatic increase in mEPSC amplitude, indicating that BDNF/TrkB signaling is exclusively involved in regulation of presynaptic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Figures 3B-F.

claim: BDNF/TrkB signaling is exclusively involved in regulation of presynaptic function during homeostatic plasticity.
source: Deletion of either BDNF or TrkB pre- or postsynaptically did not affect the homeostatic increase in mEPSC amplitude, indicating that BDNF/TrkB signaling is exclusively involved in regulation of presynaptic function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing selective effects on frequency but not amplitude.

claim: The locations of action for BDNF and TrkB are consistent with the postsynaptic initiation of RA synthesis followed by RARα-mediated translational regulation supporting retrograde BDNF signaling through presynaptic TrkB.
source: The locations of action for BDNF and TrkB are consistent with the postsynaptic initiation of RA synthesis followed by RARα-mediated translational regulation supporting the notion that retrograde BDNF signaling through presynaptic TrkB drives presynaptic changes during homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental results, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BDNF has diverse roles in synapse function and plasticity and is implicated in the pathophysiology of various brain disorders.
source: BDNF has diverse roles in synapse function and plasticity and is implicated in the pathophysiology of various brain disorders (Lima Giacobbo et al., 2019; Bathina and Das, 2015; Jin et al., 2019; Paredes et al., 2022; Autry and Monteggia, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The transcription, synthesis, and secretion of BDNF are highly activity-dependent.
source: As one of the key trans-synaptic signaling molecules, the transcription, synthesis, and secretion of BDNF are highly activity-dependent (Wong et al., 2015; Vermehren-Schmaedick et al., 2015; Miyasaka and Yamamoto, 2021; Kohara et al., 2001; Horvath et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Activity-dependent property of BDNF expression and secretion plays important roles in synapse development and remodeling.
source: This activity-dependent property of BDNF expression and secretion plays important roles in synapse development and remodeling (Hu et al., 2005; Choo et al., 2017; Yoshii and Constantine-Paton, 2010; Je et al., 2013; Gottmann et al., 2009; Bamji et al., 2006; Wong-Riley, 2021; Genoud et al., 2004; Shen and Cowan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: BDNF signaling impacts synaptic function through its actions on both inhibitory and excitatory synapses.
source: Moreover, through its actions on both inhibitory and excitatory synapses, BDNF signaling impacts synaptic function (Rauti et al., 2020; West, 2008; Lu, 2003; Karpova, 2014; Crozier et al., 2008), activity-dependent synaptic plasticity mechanisms such as long-term potentiation and long-term depression (Lu et al., 2008; Panja and Bramham, 2014; Aicardi et al., 2004; Garad et al., 2021; Aarse et al., 2016; Gangarossa et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2014), and ultimately learning and memory formation (Leal et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Cunha et al., 2010; Bekinschtein et al., 2014; Bekinschtein et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: BDNF signaling impacts activity-dependent synaptic plasticity mechanisms such as long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
source: Moreover, through its actions on both inhibitory and excitatory synapses, BDNF signaling impacts synaptic function (Rauti et al., 2020; West, 2008; Lu, 2003; Karpova, 2014; Crozier et al., 2008), activity-dependent synaptic plasticity mechanisms such as long-term potentiation and long-term depression (Lu et al., 2008; Panja and Bramham, 2014; Aicardi et al., 2004; Garad et al., 2021; Aarse et al., 2016; Gangarossa et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2014), and ultimately learning and memory formation (Leal et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Cunha et al., 2010; Bekinschtein et al., 2014; Bekinschtein et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: BDNF signaling impacts learning and memory formation.
source: Moreover, through its actions on both inhibitory and excitatory synapses, BDNF signaling impacts synaptic function (Rauti et al., 2020; West, 2008; Lu, 2003; Karpova, 2014; Crozier et al., 2008), activity-dependent synaptic plasticity mechanisms such as long-term potentiation and long-term depression (Lu et al., 2008; Panja and Bramham, 2014; Aicardi et al., 2004; Garad et al., 2021; Aarse et al., 2016; Gangarossa et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2014), and ultimately learning and memory formation (Leal et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Cunha et al., 2010; Bekinschtein et al., 2014; Bekinschtein et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: In visual cortical pyramidal neurons, exogenous BDNF blocks homeostatic upscaling induced by chronic synaptic inactivity.
source: In visual cortical pyramidal neurons, exogenous BDNF blocks homeostatic upscaling induced by chronic synaptic inactivity while BDNF depletion with TrkB-IgG scales up mEPSC amplitudes (Rutherford et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rutherford et al., 1998.

claim: BDNF depletion with TrkB-IgG scales up mEPSC amplitudes in visual cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: In visual cortical pyramidal neurons, exogenous BDNF blocks homeostatic upscaling induced by chronic synaptic inactivity while BDNF depletion with TrkB-IgG scales up mEPSC amplitudes (Rutherford et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rutherford et al., 1998.

claim: Chronic treatment of BDNF does not downscale mEPSCs in visual cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: While these results suggest a potential involvement of BDNF signaling in cortical pyramidal neuron homeostatic plasticity, chronic treatment of BDNF does not downscale mEPSCs (Leslie et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leslie et al., 2001.

claim: BDNF increases mEPSC amplitudes in visual cortical interneurons.
source: Different from its effect on cortical pyramidal cells, BDNF increases mEPSC amplitudes in visual cortical interneurons (Rutherford et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rutherford et al., 1998.

claim: In the hippocampus, BDNF enhances mEPSC amplitudes without affecting their frequencies.
source: In the hippocampus, BDNF enhances mEPSC amplitudes without affecting their frequencies, but increases mIPSC frequency and sizes of GABAergic synaptic terminals (Bolton et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bolton et al., 2000.

claim: In the hippocampus, BDNF increases mIPSC frequency and sizes of GABAergic synaptic terminals.
source: In the hippocampus, BDNF enhances mEPSC amplitudes without affecting their frequencies, but increases mIPSC frequency and sizes of GABAergic synaptic terminals (Bolton et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bolton et al., 2000.

claim: In nucleus accumbens medium spiny neurons, acute BDNF treatment (30 min) increases surface AMPAR expression.
source: In nucleus accumbens medium spiny neurons, acute BDNF treatment (30 min) increases surface AMPAR expression, but chronic BDNF treatment (24 hr) decreases surface AMPAR expression and blocks synaptic downscaling (Reimers et al., 2014; Li and Wolf, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reimers et al., 2014 and Li and Wolf, 2011.

claim: In nucleus accumbens medium spiny neurons, chronic BDNF treatment (24 hr) decreases surface AMPAR expression and blocks synaptic downscaling.
source: In nucleus accumbens medium spiny neurons, acute BDNF treatment (30 min) increases surface AMPAR expression, but chronic BDNF treatment (24 hr) decreases surface AMPAR expression and blocks synaptic downscaling (Reimers et al., 2014; Li and Wolf, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reimers et al., 2014 and Li and Wolf, 2011.

claim: BDNF's effect on synaptic transmission is multifaceted and dependent on the context of the study (cell type, brain region, developmental stage, etc.).
source: Taken together, it becomes apparent that BDNF signaling is complex as its effect on synaptic transmission is multifaceted and dependent on the context of the study (cell type, brain region, developmental stage, etc.) (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the diverse effects of BDNF described in previous studies, with citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: Endogenous BDNF signaling is required for both synaptic upscaling and downscaling in hippocampal neurons.
source: In addition to studies examining the impact of exogenous BDNF on basal synaptic transmission, the involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in homeostatic synaptic plasticity has been further investigated and found to be required for both synaptic upscaling and downscaling in hippocampal neurons (Lindskog et al., 2010; Jakawich et al., 2010; Horvath et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lindskog et al., 2010; Jakawich et al., 2010; Horvath et al., 2021.

claim: In synaptic hyperactivity-induced synaptic downscaling, mIPSC blockade and postsynaptic increase in calcium influx induce postsynaptic increase in Bdnf transcription, which mediates homeostatic down-regulation of mEPSC amplitudes.
source: In the case of synaptic hyperactivity-induced synaptic downscaling, mIPSC blockade and postsynaptic increase in calcium influx were found to induce postsynaptic increase in Bdnf transcription, which mediates homeostatic down-regulation of mEPSC amplitudes (Horvath et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath et al., 2021.

claim: In synaptic upscaling, postsynaptic release of BDNF as a retrograde messenger is required in synaptic activity blockade-induced homeostatic increase in presynaptic vesicle turnover.
source: Paradoxically, in the case of synaptic upscaling, postsynaptic release of BDNF as a retrograde messenger was also required in synaptic activity blockade-induced homeostatic increase in presynaptic vesicle turnover (Lindskog et al., 2010) and mEPSC frequency (Jakawich et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lindskog et al., 2010.

claim: Postsynaptic release of BDNF as a retrograde messenger is required in synaptic activity blockade-induced homeostatic increase in mEPSC frequency.
source: Paradoxically, in the case of synaptic upscaling, postsynaptic release of BDNF as a retrograde messenger was also required in synaptic activity blockade-induced homeostatic increase in presynaptic vesicle turnover (Lindskog et al., 2010) and mEPSC frequency (Jakawich et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jakawich et al., 2010.

claim: Rapid activation of dendritic mTORC1 signaling is a molecular mechanism for protein synthesis-dependent release of postsynaptic BDNF to mediate presynaptic homeostatic compensation under prolonged inactivation of postsynaptic AMPARs.
source: Furthermore, rapid activation of dendritic mTORC1 signaling was proposed to be a molecular mechanism for protein synthesis-dependent release of postsynaptic BDNF to mediate presynaptic homeostatic compensation under prolonged inactivation of postsynaptic AMPARs (Henry et al., 2012; Henry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henry et al., 2012 and Henry et al., 2018.

claim: At the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, postsynaptic TOR activation is required for the retrograde signaling that initiates presynaptic changes in response to reduced postsynaptic responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, where robust homeostatic increase in presynaptic release occurs in response to reduced postsynaptic responsiveness, postsynaptic TOR activation is also required for the retrograde signaling that initiates the presynaptic changes (Penney et al., 2012; Goel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Penney et al., 2012 and Goel et al., 2017.

claim: Vertebrate and invertebrate synapses share a common requirement of upstream TOR/mTOR-dependent translational activation in the postsynaptic compartment for presynaptic homeostatic plasticity.
source: Thus, although retrograde messenger systems participating in presynaptic homeostatic plasticity are likely distinct between vertebrate and invertebrate synapses, they nonetheless share a common requirement of upstream TOR/mTOR-dependent translational activation in the postsynaptic compartment, and a common functional outcome – the enhanced presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing vertebrate and invertebrate systems.

claim: Vertebrate and invertebrate synapses share a common functional outcome of enhanced presynaptic release probability in presynaptic homeostatic plasticity.
source: Thus, although retrograde messenger systems participating in presynaptic homeostatic plasticity are likely distinct between vertebrate and invertebrate synapses, they nonetheless share a common requirement of upstream TOR/mTOR-dependent translational activation in the postsynaptic compartment, and a common functional outcome – the enhanced presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing vertebrate and invertebrate systems.

claim: RARα clamps mTOR's activity level during neuronal activation through inhibition of ERK.
source: A previous study unexpectedly discovered that RARα clamps mTOR's activity level during neuronal activation through inhibition of ERK (Hsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2019.

claim: The vastly diverse functions of BDNF in the nervous system have been attributed to tight spatial, temporal, and stimulus-dependent regulation of BDNF expression from its complex gene structure.
source: The vastly diverse functions of BDNF in the nervous system have been attributed to tight spatial, temporal, and stimulus-dependent regulation of BDNF expression from its complex gene structure.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about BDNF regulation.

claim: A single Bdnf gene could give rise to several different transcripts using a combination of individual promoters and polyadenylation sites.
source: Using a combination of individual promoters (served by initial eight non-coding exons in rodents) and polyadenylation sites, a single Bdnf gene could give rise to several different transcripts (Aid et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aid et al., 2007.

claim: Most individual Bdnf promoters respond differentially to neuronal activity.
source: Although it is widely accepted that most of these individual Bdnf promoters respond differentially to neuronal activity, the specific functional roles of most of these transcripts remain elusive.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Promoter/exon IV is robustly involved in activity-dependent BDNF expression in the cortex.
source: For instance, multiple studies have shown that promoter/exon IV is robustly involved in activity-dependent BDNF expression in the cortex (Timmusk et al., 1993; Zheng et al., 2011; Sakata et al., 2013; Martinowich et al., 2011; Ratnu et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: BDNF expression driven by promoter/exon I, III, and VI is regulated by AP1 transcription factors and by TrkB signaling in a positive feedback loop.
source: In addition, BDNF expression driven by promoter/exon I, III, and VI has been shown to be regulated by AP1 transcription factors and by TrkB signaling in a positive feedback loop (West, 2008; Tuvikene et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to West, 2008 and Tuvikene et al., 2016.

claim: Dendritically localized Bdnf transcripts containing exon II and VI are subjected to RA/RARα-mediated regulation of synthesis in the postsynaptic compartment under chronic synaptic activity blockade.
source: We found that dendritically localized Bdnf transcripts containing exon II and VI are subjected to RA/RARα-mediated regulation of synthesis in the postsynaptic compartment under chronic synaptic activity blockade.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-binding assays and synaptoneurosome experiments.

claim: Newly synthesized BDNF acts retrogradely on presynaptic TrkB receptors to mediate homeostatic modulation of presynaptic function.
source: These newly synthesized BDNF acts retrogradely on presynaptic TrkB receptors to mediate homeostatic modulation of presynaptic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout experiments.

claim: An increase in Bdnf transcription and enhanced dendritic targeting of specific Bdnf transcripts have been associated with increased neuronal and synaptic activity.
source: An increase in Bdnf transcription and enhanced dendritic targeting of specific Bdnf transcripts have been associated with increased neuronal and synaptic activity (Miyasaka and Yamamoto, 2021; Horvath et al., 2021; Shimada et al., 1998; Tongiorgi et al., 1997; An et al., 2008; Verpelli et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: By acting on specific dendritically targeted Bdnf transcripts, RA/RARα selectively activates BDNF synthesis in postsynaptic compartments during synaptic inactivity.
source: Our study shows that by acting on specific dendritically targeted Bdnf transcripts, RA/RARα selectively activates BDNF synthesis in postsynaptic compartments during synaptic inactivity, thus further extending the molecular regulatory mechanisms underlying BDNF signaling in synaptic inactivity-induced synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results of this study.

claim: The human BDNF gene has a complex structure with multiple transcription initiation sites and alternative transcripts.
source: Similar to the rodent Bdnf gene, the human BDNF gene has a complex structure with multiple transcription initiation sites and alternative transcripts (Pruunsild et al., 2007), and is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders (Wang et al., 2022; Autry and Monteggia, 2012; Cattaneo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pruunsild et al., 2007.

claim: The human BDNF gene is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Similar to the rodent Bdnf gene, the human BDNF gene has a complex structure with multiple transcription initiation sites and alternative transcripts (Pruunsild et al., 2007), and is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders (Wang et al., 2022; Autry and Monteggia, 2012; Cattaneo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022; Autry and Monteggia, 2012; Cattaneo et al., 2016.

claim: The involvement of synaptic RA/RARα signaling in various neuropsychiatric diseases has begun to emerge in recent years.
source: The involvement of synaptic RA/RARα signaling in various neuropsychiatric diseases has begun to emerge in recent years (Crofton et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Suzuki, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies (Crofton et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Suzuki, 2021).

claim: The absence of RA-RARα-regulated homeostatic plasticity mechanisms has been established in Fmr1 knockout mice (a mouse model for fragile X syndrome).
source: In particular, the absence of RA-RARα-regulated homeostatic plasticity mechanisms have been established in both Fmr1 knockout mice (a mouse model for fragile X syndrome [FXS]) and human neurons differentiated from FXS patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2018.

claim: The absence of RA-RARα-regulated homeostatic plasticity mechanisms has been established in human neurons differentiated from FXS patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: In particular, the absence of RA-RARα-regulated homeostatic plasticity mechanisms have been established in both Fmr1 knockout mice (a mouse model for fragile X syndrome [FXS]) and human neurons differentiated from FXS patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2018.

claim: The convergence of BDNF signaling and RA signaling for synaptic functions and homeostatic plasticity highlights the importance of understanding the intersections of various synaptic signaling pathways and their implications in cognitive function.
source: The convergence of BDNF signaling and RA signaling for synaptic functions and homeostatic plasticity highlights the importance of understanding the intersections of various synaptic signaling pathways and their implications in cognitive function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the findings of this study and their broader implications.
